lesson.grammar_point: predictions and certainty: will / won’t (sure), be likely to / be unlikely to (probable), may / might (possible); I think... will, I don’t think... will

listenings.text: Every year, people ask me for predictions, so here are three for the next ten years. First, and I'm almost sure about this one, everybody will have a personal assistant on their phone that can book a table, answer emails and organize a trip. Second, driverless cars are likely to be common in some cities, but not everywhere. Roads and laws change slowly. And third, my least certain prediction: we might work only four days a week. If machines do more of the repetitive work, it's possible. But honestly, I wouldn't bet on it.

In our hospital, we've been using an AI tool for about two years. It looks at X-rays and shows me areas that might be a problem. It's incredibly fast. It can look at a thousand images while I look at ten. But it's not always accurate, so I still check everything myself. Will AI replace doctors? I don't think it will. It will help us, and it will probably help us find some diseases earlier. But when people are sick and scared, they want to talk to a person. No machine is likely to do that part of the job well.

My students use AI every day. They ask it to explain difficult ideas, they practice conversation with it, and they use it to check their writing. Is that a problem? Not necessarily. It can be a wonderful tool. But I'm worried about one thing. Students might stop thinking for themselves. If a machine always gives you the answer, why think? So in my class, I'm changing what I teach. I think the most important skill will be asking good questions, and checking if the answer is true. Those skills are unlikely to go out of fashion.

paras: Ten years ago, few people talked to a chatbot. Today, millions use one every day to write emails, plan trips or summarize long documents. Experts say this is just the beginning. In the next ten years, artificial intelligence will probably automate many repetitive tasks in offices, hospitals and banks. Some jobs are likely to disappear, and new ones will appear, as happened with every technological breakthrough in history.

But will machines replace people? Most experts think it is unlikely, at least in jobs that need human skills: listening, leading a team, understanding emotions, making difficult decisions. AI learns from huge amounts of data, and its answers are fast, but they are not always reliable or accurate. It might give you a perfect summary, or it might invent a fact with total confidence. That is why people will still need to check its work.

So what should we do? The most useful skill, experts say, will be learning. Technology changes so fast that nobody can know everything, but everybody can try to keep up with it. People who learn to use these tools well are likely to have an advantage. And, interestingly, many experts think the most human skills, like communication in other languages, might become more valuable, not less.
